split.label: Watch Liz Rice, "Containers From Scratch" (GOTO 2018, ~43 min) up to the chroot step — clone() and the namespace flags, live-coded in Go.
Finish the talk — chroot/pivot_root and cgroups — then re-run her commands yourself in a scratch VM or container.
Read OSTEP (free) Ch 4 "The Abstraction: The Process" (~15 pp): the process API, the state machine, and the list of what a process actually is.
Read OSTEP Ch 26 "Concurrency: An Introduction" (~18 pp): threads share the address space, but each gets its own stack.
Read Docker Multi-stage builds: COPY --from to ship only the built binary, leaving the toolchain behind.
Read Docker build best practices: order steps by change-frequency (deps before source) so the layer cache actually hits.
Read HPBN (free) "Building Blocks of TCP" — the whole chapter.
Then the short "Building Blocks of UDP" chapter — what TCP gives you that UDP doesn’t.
Skim the workload objects: Pod and Deployment→ReplicaSet→Pod.
Then the networking & config objects: Service (stable VIP + label selector), Ingress, ConfigMap/Secret.
Read PostgreSQL docs 14.1 "Using EXPLAIN" — the whole section, running each example.
Then UTIL’s Postgres execution plans — the same output read by someone hunting a slow query.
Read the k8s scheduler — filter → score → bind.
Then liveness/readiness/startup probes — three probes, three different jobs.
Read requests/limits.
Then the HorizontalPodAutoscaler — what it scales on, and why it needs requests to be set.
Skim the OWASP Top 10 (2025 — the current edition), entries #1–#5: Broken Access Control, Security Misconfiguration, Software Supply-Chain Failures, Cryptographic Failures, Injection.
Then entries #6–#10 of the same list — one line each on what the category means and the one defense that kills most of it.
Read PostgreSQL docs Ch 13.1 Concurrency Control (MVCC).
Then 13.2 Transaction Isolation — the four levels and the anomalies each one still allows.
Read Martin Fowler BlueGreenDeployment (rolling is the k8s default).
Then CanaryRelease — the same cut-over, done to a slice of traffic.
Read the 4 GitOps principles.
Then The Twelve-Factor App — esp. III config in env, VI stateless, IX disposability, XI logs to stdout.
Read Mastering Ethereum (2nd ed, free) Ch 4 "Cryptography" — keys, addresses, and signing.
Then the Merkle-tree section of Mastering Bitcoin (3rd ed) Ch 11 — how a root commits to every transaction under it.
Read HPBN HTTP/1.X: persistent connections, and why pipelining failed.
Then HTTP/2: multiplexing, the binary framing layer, and HPACK.
For H3/QUIC, read the free HTTP/3 explained through the QUIC transport chapters: reliable multiplexed streams over UDP, TLS 1.3 built in.
Finish the same book: the HTTP/3 mapping itself, plus connection migration and 0-RTT.
Read the Redis FAQ — the single-thread rationale, in their own words.
Then the data types overview — strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, HLL.
Read DDIA Ch 7 "Weak Isolation Levels" as far as Snapshot Isolation (Read Committed → SI, and the reads each one can still see).
Finish DDIA Ch 7: Preventing Lost Updates, then Write Skew & Phantoms.
Read Google SRE (free) Ch 6 "Monitoring Distributed Systems" to the end of the Four Golden Signals (Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation).
Finish SRE Ch 6: choosing a resolution, keeping alerts simple, and the long-term-vs-short-term tension.
Read Mastering Ethereum Ch 14 "The EVM" — the machine, its data locations, and gas.
Then explore evm.codes — per-opcode gas in a live playground; run a few opcodes by hand.
Read DDIA Ch 11 "Messaging Systems" → "Partitioned Logs".
Then Jay Kreps’ "The Log" (archived — LinkedIn removed the original) — long, and worth it.
Read the OAuth RFC 6749 authorization-code flow (§4.1) — who redirects whom, and which secret travels on which channel.
Then PKCE (RFC 7636) — the code_challenge/code_verifier pair and the attack it closes.
Then PortSwigger’s JWT attacks lab pages — alg=none, key confusion, and unverified signatures.
Read Solana docs Accounts — everything, including code, is an account.
Then Programs — executable accounts that hold no state of their own.
Read Mastering Ethereum Ch 6 "Transactions" — the fields, RLP encoding, and the signature.
Then EIP-1559 itself — base fee, tip, and the burn.
Read Kafka: The Definitive Guide (2nd ed, free from Confluent) Ch 1 — the log, the broker, the vocabulary.
Then Kafka: The Definitive Guide’s internals chapter — the controller, replication, and how a request is handled.
Then Kafka: The Definitive Guide’s reliable data delivery chapter — acks, in-sync replicas, and what each setting costs.
Read the AWS caching patterns whitepaper page — cache-aside vs write-through vs write-behind.
Then the Redis eviction and persistence (RDB/AOF) pages — what a cache drops, and what it keeps across a restart.
Read Solana docs PDAs + CPIs — program-owned addresses, and one program calling another.
Then Compute Budget and the Sealevel runtime — the budget an instruction gets, and how the runtime parallelizes.
Read Mastering Bitcoin (3rd ed) Ch 12 "Mining and Consensus" as far as difficulty retargeting — PoW and the puzzle itself.
Finish Ch 12: assembling and validating a block, and why the best chain is the one with the most cumulative work.
Read ethereum.org Gasper — Casper FFG finality + the LMD-GHOST fork choice.
Then Vitalik’s "On Settlement Finality" — what "final" can and cannot mean.
Read the Solidity docs Security Considerations — checks-effects-interactions, and the rest of the list.
Then samczsun’s "So you want to use a price oracle" — a tour of how each naive price source gets drained.
Read the Raft paper (Extended Version) "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm" (Ongaro & Ousterhout) §5.1–§5.3 — leader election and log replication.
Finish §5 of the Raft paper: safety (the election restriction), follower/candidate crashes, and timing.
Read OSTEP (free) Ch 18 "Paging: Introduction" — page tables, and why the naive version is too slow.
Then Ch 19 "Paging: Faster Translations (TLBs)" — the cache that makes paging affordable.
Read ethereum.org Scaling — the rollup model: execute off-chain, settle on L1.
Then the same page’s optimistic-vs-ZK sections — fraud proofs (and their challenge window) vs validity proofs.
Read Confluent "Exactly-Once Semantics… Here's How Kafka Does It" — the idempotent producer half.
Finish it (the transactions half), checking the spec where it matters: KIP-98.
Skim Lamport, "Paxos Made Simple" — prepare/promise → accept, and majority quorums.
Then the Raft paper’s "What’s wrong with Paxos?" section — the same problem, argued from the other side.
Read PG docs "TOAST" — where an oversized value actually goes.
Then "Heap-Only Tuples (HOT)" — the update that skips the indexes.
Read the SPIFFE overview — a workload identity (spiffe://…) instead of a shared secret.
Then SVIDs — that identity as a short-lived, auto-rotated cert.
Read EIP-4844 — blob-carrying transactions and the separate blob-gas market.
Then the explainer eip4844.com — the same design with the diagrams.
Read the Redis Cluster spec — the 16384 hash slots and how keys map onto them.
Finish the Cluster spec: gossip between nodes, and MOVED vs ASK redirects.
Read Gilbert & Lynch, "Perspectives on the CAP Theorem" (2012) — CAP stated as a safety-vs-liveness trade.
Finish the paper: the proof sketch, and why "pick 2 of 3" is the part everyone forgets.
Read ethereum.org MEV — where the value comes from, and who extracts it.
Then Flashbots MEV-Boost — builders bid, proposers sign the best, a relay mediates.
Read OpenZeppelin "Proxy Upgrade Pattern" — delegatecall, and how storage layouts collide.
Then ERC-1967 — the standard slots that stop the collision.
Scale-out trade-offs: DDIA Ch 6 "Partitioning" as far as partitioning secondary indexes (key-range vs hash, and skew).
Finish DDIA Ch 6: rebalancing strategies and request routing.
Read RFC 9000 (QUIC transport) for the model — connection IDs, streams, and migration.
Then skim RFC 9002 — loss detection & congestion control, QUIC’s version of the TCP machinery.
Read ERC-4337 — UserOperations, bundlers, the EntryPoint, and paymasters.
Then EIP-7702 — an EOA delegating to contract code, the protocol-level shortcut.
Read SLSA — the build/source provenance levels, and what each one actually requires.
Then Sigstore — keyless signing with Cosign + Fulcio + Rekor.
Then the Saga original: Garcia-Molina & Salem, "Sagas" (1987).
Then microservices.io Saga — the same idea as people actually deploy it.
Read PG docs "High Availability… and Replication" — streaming replication, and what synchronous really costs.
Then "Logical Replication" — row-level changes over a publication/subscription, and what it can’t carry.
Read Debezium, "Reliable Microservices Data Exchange With the Outbox Pattern" — one local transaction, then the log does the rest.
Then the Outbox Event Router SMT docs — the pattern as a running piece of configuration.
Read Vitalik, "zk-SNARKs: Under the Hood" as far as the QAP — computation → circuit → R1CS → QAP.
Finish the post: the pairing check, and where the trusted setup enters.
Read antirez’s Redlock spec — the algorithm as proposed.
Then Kleppmann’s critique "How to do distributed locking" — fencing tokens, and clocks you can’t trust.
Then antirez’s rebuttal — and decide for yourself which assumption you’re willing to make.
Read "Lord of the io_uring" — the SQE/CQE ring model, submission, and completion.
Then LWN "The rapid growth of io_uring" — what it grew to cover, and the security surface that came with it.
Read the Dynamo paper, "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007) §4.1–§4.5 — consistent hashing, replication, and versioning with vector clocks.
Finish the Dynamo paper: quorums (R + W > N), hinted handoff, anti-entropy with Merkle trees, and the production lessons in §6.
Read DDIA Ch 3 "Storage and Retrieval" through SSTables & LSM-Trees.
Finish DDIA Ch 3: B-Trees, and the comparison (write/read/space amplification).
Read the Cilium "BPF and XDP Reference Guide" — maps, program types, and the hook points.
Then the eBPF docs XDP program type — packets handled before the kernel builds an skb.
Skim the kernel’s eBPF verifier doc — a static analysis that must prove termination and memory safety before your program loads.
Then the verify-then-JIT half of "What is eBPF?" — the same pipeline, end to end.
Read the Firedancer repo/README — a second validator implementation, and why that matters for client diversity.
Then the Anza docs, and follow Anza’s Alpenglow announcement for the consensus change.
Read cppreference std::memory_order — the six orderings, as specified.
Then Preshing, "Acquire and Release Semantics" — the same thing explained so it sticks.
Read the as-if rule — C/C++ "observable behavior", and everything a compiler may do around it.
Then register allocation — one concrete optimization the compiler runs on your IR.
Read Flink "Timely Stream Processing" — event time vs processing time, and watermarks.
Then the Google Dataflow model paper (Akidau et al., 2015) — what/where/when/how, the framework behind all of it.
Read Brendan Gregg: Flame Graphs — how to read one, and how to generate one.
Then perf examples — the commands you would actually run on a hot box.
Then eBPF tracing tools — the same questions answered with far less overhead.
Read EIP-712 — typed structured signing and the domain separator that binds a signature to one contract and chain.
Then EIP-2612 permit — the same machinery used to replace an approve transaction.
Read V8’s "Launching Ignition and TurboFan" — the interpreter/optimizer pair, and why both exist.
Then skim Maglev — the mid-tier added between Sparkplug and TurboFan, and what it is for.
Read the Go GC guide — the knobs, and the cost model behind them.
Then Rick Hudson’s "Getting to Go" — a real low-latency concurrent collector, and what it took.
Read Doug Lea’s "A Memory Allocator" — dlmalloc, the design behind glibc.
Then Google’s tcmalloc design — per-thread caches and size classes, for the multithreaded case.
Read floating-point-gui.de for the intuition — why the format can’t hold 0.1.
Then skim Goldberg’s canonical "What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic" — rounding, guard digits, and cancellation.
Read the Java Virtual Machine Guide — HotSpot compilation, as the vendor documents it.
Then OpenJDK’s HotSpot wiki — tiered compilation and deoptimization.
Read Joel Spolsky’s "The Absolute Minimum… about Unicode".
Then the UTF-8 Everywhere manifesto — one encoding, and the bugs that picking another one buys you.
Read the famous "Why is processing a sorted array faster?" answer.
Then Dan Luu’s branch-prediction walkthrough — how predictors actually got good.
Read the Bloom filter overview — the math, the false-positive rate, and where it is used.
Then play with the interactive visual tutorial until the bit pattern is obvious.
Read Crafting Interpreters "Scanning" — characters to tokens, and why tokens are regular.
Then "Parsing Expressions" — recursive descent, and precedence as grammar shape.
Read the "Introduction to the Go compiler" (cmd/compile README) through type-checking (also on go.dev).
Finish the README: the SSA phases and machine-code generation.
Read Crafting Interpreters "Evaluating Expressions" — walk the tree, produce a value.
Then "Statements and State" — environments and lexical scope.
Read Crafting Interpreters "Chunks of Bytecode" — a flat instruction array instead of a tree.
Then "A Virtual Machine" — the stack and the dispatch loop.
Read Static single-assignment form — why every serious optimizer converts to it.
Then register allocation — graph-colouring and linear scan.
